description: Jeremiah writes this from the far side of the worst thing that ever happened to him. The harder question is whether we can say it while we are still in the middle of it.
excerpt: That's where faithfulness gets learned. Not on the far side of the hard thing, but right in the middle of it.
verse: "I will never forget this awful time, as I grieve over my loss. Yet I still dare to hope when I remember this: The faithful love of the Lord never ends! His mercies never cease. Great is his faithfulness; his mercies begin afresh each morning. I say to myself, 'The Lord is my inheritance; therefore, I will hope in him!'"Lamentations 3:20-24 (NLT)"So it is good to wait quietly for salvation from the Lord."
body_html:
Jeremiah is writing this in the middle of grief. Jerusalem has fallen. Everything he warned about actually happened. And right in the middle of that pain, he looks up and says, God's mercies begin afresh every morning. Great is His faithfulness.

Anyone who's walked with God for any length of time has stood in that same place. Looking back over a horrible season and being able to say, God was faithful through all of it.

A few years ago I felt like I wanted a word for the year. I was praying about it, asking God what word He wanted to show me. Faithfulness kept coming up. But it wasn't just about looking back and seeing all He'd done, which is honestly the easier version. It's about knowing He's faithful today. That's the harder part.

Jeremiah's writing this from the other side. He's already through the worst of it. He can look back and name the mercies. He can see the faithfulness because it's in the rearview.

The real test is whether we can say the same thing while we're still in it.

Can I say God is faithful today, in the middle of the storm, before I can see how any of it is going to work out? Can I trust that His mercies are new this morning even when this morning still feels heavy? Can I hold onto Romans 8:28, that God works all things together for good for those who love Him, when the "all things" haven't been worked out yet?

That's where faithfulness gets learned. Not on the far side of the hard thing, but right in the middle of it.

Verse 26 makes it even more direct. It is good to wait quietly for salvation from the Lord. Quiet waiting is hard. Loud waiting comes naturally to most of us. Panicking, planning, complaining, talking it through with everyone we know. Quiet waiting means trusting Him enough to not fill the silence with our own noise.

The faithfulness we celebrate looking back was built in seasons of waiting we didn't want to be in. And the trust we'll have in future storms is being built right now in whatever we're walking through today.

His mercies are new this morning. Even this morning. Even if this morning is hard.

Where in your life do you need to trust God's faithfulness today, before you're on the other side of the hard thing?
question: Where in your life do you need to trust God's faithfulness today, before you're on the other side of the hard thing?
